verses.text: I wish that you would bear with me in a little foolishness, but indeed you do bear with me.
For I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy. For I married you to one husband, that I might present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
But I am afraid that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness, so your minds might be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.

For if he who comes preaches another Jesus, whom we did not preach, or if you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive, or a different “good news”, which you did not accept, you put up with that well enough.
For I reckon that I am not at all behind the very best apostles.
But though I am unskilled in speech, yet I am not unskilled in knowledge. No, in every way we have been revealed to you in all things.
Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself that you might be exalted, because I preached to you God’s Good News free of charge?
I robbed other assemblies, taking wages from them that I might serve you.

When I was present with you and was in need, I wasn’t a burden on anyone, for the brothers, when they came from Macedonia, supplied the measure of my need. In everything I kept myself from being burdensome to you, and I will continue to do so.
As the truth of Christ is in me, no one will stop me from this boasting in the regions of Achaia.
Why? Because I don’t love you? God knows.
But what I do, that I will do, that I may cut off occasion from them that desire an occasion, that in which they boast, they may be found even as we.
For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as Christ’s apostles.
And no wonder, for even Satan masquerades as an angel of light.
It is no great thing therefore if his servants also masquerade as servants of righteousness, whose end will be according to their works.
I say again, let no one think me foolish. But if so, yet receive me as foolish, that I also may boast a little.
That which I speak, I don’t speak according to the Lord, but as in foolishness, in this confidence of boasting.
Seeing that many boast after the flesh, I will also boast.
For you bear with the foolish gladly, being wise.
For you bear with a man, if he brings you into bondage, if he devours you, if he takes you captive, if he exalts himself, if he strikes you on the face.
I speak by way of disparagement, as though we had been weak. Yet in whatever way anyone is bold (I speak in foolishness), I am bold also.
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they the offspring  of Abraham? So am I.
Are they servants of Christ? (I speak as one beside himself) I am more so; in labors more abundantly, in prisons more abundantly, in stripes above measure, in deaths often.
Five times from the Jews I received forty stripes minus one.
Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I suffered shipwreck. I have been a night and a day in the deep.

I have been in travels often, perils of rivers, perils of robbers, perils from my countrymen, perils from the Gentiles, perils in the city, perils in the wilderness, perils in the sea, perils among false brothers;
in labor and travail, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, and in cold and nakedness.
Besides those things that are outside, there is that which presses on me daily, anxiety for all the assemblies.
Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is caused to stumble, and I don’t burn with indignation?
If I must boast, I will boast of the things that concern my weakness.
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, he who is blessed forever more, knows that I don’t lie.
In Damascus the governor under King Aretas guarded the city of the Damascenes desiring to arrest me.
Through a window I was let down in a basket by the wall, and escaped his hands.

footnotes.content: Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with him in a little foolishness. Notice his politeness—even as he's about to defend himself hard, he asks their patience first. That's the mark of a true shepherd: you don't demand; you ask.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I married you to one husband"—Paul borrows the language of betrothal. He speaks as the friend of the bridegroom (John 3:29), jealous for the bride's fidelity to Christ alone. His passion here is not possessive; it's protective.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The serpent deceived Eve in her simplicity. Paul sees the same danger now: a corruption of the simple faith in Christ. All false teaching works the same way—it muddles what is plain and true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul names what the Corinthians have tolerated: a different Jesus, a different spirit, a different gospel. He's astonished they've been so patient with what they shouldn't bear at all. Sometimes tolerance becomes a weakness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I am not at all behind the very best apostles." Paul says this plainly—not in anger, but in simple fact. He knows his apostolic authority. There's a kind of humility that also knows its own truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Unskilled in speech, but not in knowledge. Paul doesn't apologize for plain words. The Corinthians know him—they've seen his life and work in every way. That's more convincing than eloquence ever was.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He preached God's Good News free of charge and humbled himself so they might be exalted. He's asking: How can this be a sin? Yet they questioned him for it. Love often pays a price nobody asked it to.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He "robbed" other churches of his presence and labor so he could serve Corinth free. That's the language of sacrifice—he took what belonged elsewhere and gave it to them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the Macedonians came with help, it freed him from being a burden. He kept that vow—to serve without taking. Some will call you poor for it. Call it faithfulness instead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "As the truth of Christ is in me, no one will stop me." Paul swears by the truth—by Christ himself. He will not shrink from this boasting in his own weakness and sufferings.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why? Because I don't love you?" The question hangs in the air. His whole defense rests on love. If you question his words, you haven't questioned his heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul cuts off the occasion for false apostles to boast. He will show himself equal to them, not by mimicking their vice but by matching their labor in the gospel. Do good so plainly that lies have nowhere to hide.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: False apostles are deceitful workers masquerading as Christ's apostles. Paul doesn't mince words. He names the danger plainly because the flock deserves to know who the wolves are.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even Satan masquerades as an angel of light. This is ancient wisdom—the enemy's greatest trick is to look like the good. It's why we must know the true light ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Satan's servants masquerade as servants of righteousness, but their end will be according to their works. In the end, the mask comes off. Works tell the truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul asks them not to think him foolish—yet if they do, receive him as foolish so he can boast a little. There's a tender humor here beneath the defense. He needs them to understand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He speaks not according to the Lord, but in foolishness and boasting. Paul is careful to say: this catalog of my sufferings—it's not the Lord's way. I am doing this only to match their insistence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Seeing that many boast after the flesh, I will also boast." But watch—his boasting won't be about flesh. It's about weakness and suffering. His folly will expose theirs as truly foolish.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You bear with the foolish gladly, being wise. There's irony here—they pride themselves on wisdom while tolerating false teachers. Discernment begins by asking: Who really feeds my soul?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You bear with men who bring you into bondage, devour you, take you captive, exalt themselves, strike your face. The catalog is blunt: false teachers abuse authority. Look for gentleness and humility as the marks of a true shepherd.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul speaks as one beside himself—in whatever way anyone is bold, he is bold also. Yet his boldness is in the cross, in weakness, in what it cost him to love them. That is a different boldness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Are they Hebrews? Israelites? Offspring of Abraham? So am I. Paul claims his pedigree—not to boast in flesh, but to show he speaks from deep in the tradition. He is not an outsider.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In labors more abundantly, in prisons more abundantly, in stripes above measure, in deaths often. Paul lists what it cost to serve Christ. This is his boasting—not power, but the price of love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five times from the Jews he received forty stripes minus one—a precise, terrible number. The law allowed forty; mercy stopped at thirty-nine. Even torture has its measure in Scripture.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beaten with rods, stoned, shipwrecked three times, a night and day in the deep. Paul catalogs horrors as plainly as listing groceries. When you've suffered for the gospel, you stop embellishing it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Perils of rivers, robbers, countrymen, Gentiles, city, wilderness, sea, and false brothers too. He lists every danger—and the betrayal of false brothers wounds deeper than any storm.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Labor, travail, watchings often, hunger, thirst, fastings, cold, nakedness. The list goes on—the body worn down to nothing. Yet Paul doesn't complain; he simply witnesses to the cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Beyond the external pressures, there is that which presses on him daily: anxiety for all the assemblies. The deepest burden is not pain but love—the care for every flock.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who stumbles, and I don't burn with indignation? This is the pastor's heart—your weakness becomes his, your stumbling ignites his righteous grief.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this verse: boasting of weakness rather than strength, counting loss as gain, finding glory in the cross. It runs counter to everything the world teaches—and yet it is the deepest truth we know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul swears by God and Father of the Lord Jesus that he doesn't lie. He calls heaven itself as witness. The truth matters enough to stake his eternity on it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In Damascus the governor under King Aretas guarded the city, desiring to arrest him. This is a real memory—Paul lived this. History witnessed his danger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Through a window he was let down in a basket by the wall and escaped. The great apostle's flight in a basket—unglamorous, undignified, but alive and faithful. That is enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
